title: Manoj Bajpayee Had to Google 'Balance of Payments' to Play India's Most Powerful Banker. The Film Opens Thursday.
excerpt: Governor revisits the night India pawned its gold to survive — and Bajpayee taught himself economics one search at a time to make you believe it.
body:
There's a scene in **Governor** that **Manoj Bajpayee** calls his favourite, and it has nothing to do with gold reserves, foreign exchange, or the balance of payments. It's a quiet conversation between the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India and his wife, at home, about how families prepare for hard times — and how nations should, too.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=Mvm0bRY0Qyg</youtube>

> "Sometimes, the biggest advice or lessons comes not from experts; we get it from our homes." — Manoj Bajpayee

It's the most Bajpayee answer imaginable: find the human frequency in a story about institutional crisis. And that instinct is exactly why he's the only actor in Hindi cinema who could make a film about the 1991 economic collapse feel like something you'd actually want to watch on a Thursday evening.

Governor, directed by **Chinmay Mandlekar** and releasing in cinemas on June 12, is based on one of the most dramatic and least-told stories in modern Indian history. In 1990, as Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait sent oil prices spiralling and remittances from the Gulf dried up overnight, India's foreign exchange reserves fell to levels that could barely cover two weeks of imports. The country was, quite literally, weeks from defaulting on its international obligations.

Enter **S. Venkitaramanan**, the real-life RBI Governor who authorised one of the most controversial emergency measures in Indian economic history: the physical shipment of India's gold reserves to London, pledged as collateral to secure approximately $405 million in emergency loans. It was a desperate, humiliating, and ultimately genius act of survival — one that bought India enough time to launch the liberalisation reforms of 1991. The same reforms that, three decades later, built the economy that sent millions of Indians to careers in New York, London, Toronto, and the Bay Area.

Bajpayee plays a fictionalised version of Venkitaramanan named A. Ramanan, and his preparation was characteristically intense — and disarmingly honest.

> "I was very bad in economics. For every scene and dialogue, I had to search the terms online because as an actor, everything I deliver has to be believable. What does it mean that we have a deficit balance of 1.5 billion if I didn't understand it?" — Manoj Bajpayee

The man Googled 'deficit balance' before every take. And somehow, that makes you trust him more — because if Bajpayee doesn't coast through a performance, you know the character won't coast through the crisis either.

The supporting cast signals serious intent. **Adah Sharma**, **Madhoo Shah**, and **Noushad Mohamed Kunju** round out the ensemble. The score is by **Amit Trivedi** with lyrics from the legendary **Javed Akhtar** — a pairing that alone tells you the makers aren't treating this like a history textbook. Mandlekar, who established himself in Marathi cinema with a sharp eye for political complexity and institutional drama, brings a director's sensibility that's fast, dense, and obsessed with the mechanics of power.

What makes Governor especially compelling for diaspora audiences isn't just the history lesson — it's the personal resonance. If you're an NRI over 40, you likely remember the 1991 crisis firsthand: the import restrictions, the queues, the whispered conversations about India possibly defaulting. If you're younger, this is the origin story of the India you actually grew up in — the one with Infosys and IT corridors and middle-class prosperity. Governor is telling you how close the whole thing came to not happening at all.

The marketing has been shrewd, too. In a move that's equal parts nostalgic and provocative, the makers announced that the **first 25,000 tickets on BookMyShow** will be sold at 1990s prices. "The story is historic and the ticket prices too," the official caption read. It's a gimmick, sure — but it's a good one. And it underlines the film's central provocation: you're watching in 2026, but you're paying what the country was worth in 1990.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZaBOTKoLxN/

The timing feels almost scripted. With a reported blockade at the Strait of Hormuz triggering a fresh global fuel crisis, a weaker rupee, and early tremors of an oil squeeze, Governor arrives in a moment that feels less like period drama and more like a mirror. Bajpayee himself has leaned into the parallel: "The world is going through a major conflict. In 2008, the world was affected by a massive recession. Still, we came out of it. As a countryman, I have faith."

The CBFC cleared the film with a **U/A 16+** rating and zero cuts — a welcome surprise in a week where the censor board has been drawing fire for heavy-handed interventions elsewhere. Runtime is a tight 127 minutes.

Governor opens in cinemas across India on **Thursday, June 12**. It's a rare Bollywood film that asks you to care about monetary policy and gold reserves and balance sheets — and with Bajpayee at the centre, looking like he's carrying the weight of a nation on his shoulders, you probably will. For the diaspora, this one is personal. The crisis that nearly broke India is the same one that built your life abroad.
